claim: RNAi is prone to off-target effects.
source: Specifically, RNAi is prone to off-target effects (Jackson et al., 2003; Scacheri et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Jackson et al., 2003; Scacheri et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2005).

claim: RNAi is associated with insufficient knockdown levels.
source: Specifically, RNAi is prone to off-target effects (Jackson et al., 2003; Scacheri et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2005) and insufficient knockdown levels
evidence: The claim is stated as a known limitation of RNAi technology, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based methods are associated with off-target effects.
source: while CRISPR/Cas9-based methods are associated with off-target effects and incomplete LOF across cell populations
evidence: The claim is stated as a known limitation of CRISPR/Cas9 technology, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based methods are associated with incomplete loss-of-function across cell populations.
source: while CRISPR/Cas9-based methods are associated with off-target effects and incomplete LOF across cell populations
evidence: The claim is stated as a known limitation of CRISPR/Cas9 technology, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Optimized micro-RNA embedded shRNAs in the miR-E backbone do not interfere with endogenous miRNA processing.
source: As suitable RNAi system, we chose optimized micro-RNA embedded shRNAs (shRNAmirs) in the miR-E backbone (Fellmann et al., 2013), which do not interfere with endogenous miRNA processing (Premsrirut et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Premsrirut et al., 2011.

claim: shRNAmirs in the miR-E backbone can be expressed from tet-responsive elements and other Pol-II promoters in the 3′-UTR of fluorescent reporter genes.
source: which do not interfere with endogenous miRNA processing (Premsrirut et al., 2011) and can be expressed from tet-responsive elements and other Pol-II promoters in the 3′-UTR of fluorescent reporter genes, thus providing a versatile system for inducible RNAi (Zuber et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zuber et al., 2011.

claim: The ARTi design matrix is TTCGWWWNNAHHWWCATCCGGN (W = A/T, H = A/T/C; N = A/T/G/C).
source: By merging nucleotide biases identified in both analyses, we derived a 22-nt base composition matrix for the design of ARTi shRNAmirs (TTCGWWWNNAHHWWCATCCGGN; W = A/T, H = A/T/C; N = A/T/G/C) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of nucleotide composition and is presented as a derived result.

claim: All shRNAs whose extended seed sequence (guide positions 2–14) had a perfect match in the human or mouse transcriptome were eliminated from ARTi design.
source: To further reduce possible off-target effects, we eliminated all shRNAs whose extended seed sequence (guide positions 2–14) had a perfect match in the human or mouse transcriptome and, finally, selected six top-scoring ARTi predictions for experimental validation.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological step taken by the authors to reduce off-target effects.

claim: Six top-scoring ARTi predictions were selected for experimental validation.
source: To further reduce possible off-target effects, we eliminated all shRNAs whose extended seed sequence (guide positions 2–14) had a perfect match in the human or mouse transcriptome and, finally, selected six top-scoring ARTi predictions for experimental validation.
evidence: The claim describes the authors' experimental design and selection process.

claim: All six ARTi-shRNAmirs matched or outperformed previously validated highly potent shRNAmirs targeting Renilla luciferase or PTEN.
source: In all six cases, ARTi-shRNAmir matched or outperformed previously validated highly potent shRNAmirs targeting Renilla luciferase or PTEN (Fellmann et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and comparison to previously validated shRNAmirs.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmirs ranked among top-performing shRNAmirs overall when compared to a panel of 592 gene-specific shRNAs.
source: We compared these results to a panel of 592 gene-specific shRNAs that were tested using the same assay and found that ARTi-shRNAmirs ranked among top-performing shRNAmirs overall (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing ARTi-shRNAmirs to 592 gene-specific shRNAs, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmir expression had no effects on proliferation or survival in four human and three mouse cell lines, with the exception of ARTi.6634 and ARTi.6786.
source: ARTi-shRNAmir expression had no effects on proliferation or survival in four human and three mouse cell lines (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), with the exception of ARTi.6634 and ARTi.6786, which induced a mild fitness defect in the murine leukemia cell line RN2 and MV4-11, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from competitive proliferation assays shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ARTi.6634 induced a mild fitness defect in the murine leukemia cell line RN2.
source: with the exception of ARTi.6634 and ARTi.6786, which induced a mild fitness defect in the murine leukemia cell line RN2 and MV4-11, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from competitive proliferation assays.

claim: ARTi.6786 induced a mild fitness defect in MV4-11 cells.
source: with the exception of ARTi.6634 and ARTi.6786, which induced a mild fitness defect in the murine leukemia cell line RN2 and MV4-11, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from competitive proliferation assays.

claim: Stable expression of ARTi-shRNAmirs had only marginal effects on the transcriptome in two commonly used human cell lines.
source: In contrast to the effects of a MEK inhibitor trametinib, which we included as a positive control, stable expression of ARTi-shRNAmirs had only marginal effects on the transcriptome in two commonly used human cell lines (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F)
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome profiling data shown in Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmirs do not trigger major off-target effects, even in the absence of their respective target site.
source: indicating that they do not trigger major off-target effects, even in the absence of their respective target site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptome profiling and proliferation assay data showing minimal effects.

claim: EGFR acts as a driving oncogene in various cancer types.
source: To establish ARTi as a method for target validation, we performed ARTi-based LOF experiments in cancer cell lines and xenograft models for three prominent oncology targets: EGFR and KRAS, which act as driving oncogenes in various cancer types (Hynes and MacDonald, 2009; Punekar et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hynes and MacDonald, 2009 and Punekar et al., 2022.

claim: KRAS acts as a driving oncogene in various cancer types.
source: To establish ARTi as a method for target validation, we performed ARTi-based LOF experiments in cancer cell lines and xenograft models for three prominent oncology targets: EGFR and KRAS, which act as driving oncogenes in various cancer types (Hynes and MacDonald, 2009; Punekar et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hynes and MacDonald, 2009 and Punekar et al., 2022.

claim: STAG1 has been identified as a synthetic lethal interaction with recurrent LOF mutations of STAG2.
source: and STAG1, which has been identified as a synthetic lethal interaction with recurrent LOF mutations of STAG2 (Bailey et al., 2021; van der Lelij et al., 2020; Benedetti et al., 2014; van der Lelij et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2021; van der Lelij et al., 2020; Benedetti et al., 2014; van der Lelij et al., 2017.

claim: The EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene rendered Ba/F3 cells cytokine-independent.
source: To establish an ARTi-repressible version of oncogenic EGFRdel19, we cloned ARTi-shRNAmir target sequences into an expression construct encoding EGFRdel19 fused to dsRed (Figure 2A), which rendered Ba/F3 cells cytokine-independent and sensitive to EGFR inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene rendered Ba/F3 cells sensitive to EGFR inhibition.
source: To establish an ARTi-repressible version of oncogenic EGFRdel19, we cloned ARTi-shRNAmir target sequences into an expression construct encoding EGFRdel19 fused to dsRed (Figure 2A), which rendered Ba/F3 cells cytokine-independent and sensitive to EGFR inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene fully rescued the loss of endogenous EGFRdel19 in PC-9 cells.
source: The EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene fully rescued the loss of endogenous EGFRdel19
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing functional rescue.

claim: Dox-inducible expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir resulted in an almost complete drop of reads mapping to the codon-optimized EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene.
source: Consistently, in RNA-sequencing we observed an almost complete drop of reads mapping to the codon-optimized EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene upon dox-inducible expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir, as well as a downregulation of DUSP6 and other canonical targets of RAF-MEK-ERK signaling, which acts as key effector pathway of EGFRdel19 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Dox-inducible expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir resulted in downregulation of DUSP6 and other canonical targets of RAF-MEK-ERK signaling.
source: Consistently, in RNA-sequencing we observed an almost complete drop of reads mapping to the codon-optimized EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi transgene upon dox-inducible expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir, as well as a downregulation of DUSP6 and other canonical targets of RAF-MEK-ERK signaling, which acts as key effector pathway of EGFRdel19 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: RAF-MEK-ERK signaling acts as key effector pathway of EGFRdel19.
source: as well as a downregulation of DUSP6 and other canonical targets of RAF-MEK-ERK signaling, which acts as key effector pathway of EGFRdel19 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about EGFR signaling pathways.

claim: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir led to rapid and durable tumor regression in PC-9 xenografts.
source: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir led to rapid and durable tumor regression that was indistinguishable from the effects of osimertinib (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir led to tumor regression that was indistinguishable from the effects of osimertinib in PC-9 xenografts.
source: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir led to rapid and durable tumor regression that was indistinguishable from the effects of osimertinib (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 2D comparing ARTi-shRNAmir to osimertinib treatment.

claim: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir was not observed to cause tumor regression in parental PC-9 cells that lack the ARTi target site.
source: and not observed in parental PC-9 cells that lack the ARTi target site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ARTi-induced phenotypes are to be attributed to on-target effects that predict the activity of advanced small-molecule inhibitors in vivo.
source: We therefore conclude that ARTi-induced phenotypes are to be attributed to on-target effects that predict the activity of advanced small-molecule inhibitors in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of ARTi effects to osimertinib and the lack of effects in parental cells.

claim: Switching the driving oncogene from KRASG12C to KRASG12R rendered MIA PaCa-2 cells resistant to the KRASG12C inhibitor AMG-510.
source: As expected, switching the driving oncogene from KRASG12C to KRASG12R rendered MIA PaCa-2 cells resistant to the KRASG12C inhibitor AMG-510 (Fakih et al., 2020; Lanman et al., 2020; Fakih et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and citations to studies on AMG-510.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to a strong suppression of dsRed::KRASG12R expression at the mRNA level.
source: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to a strong suppression of dsRed::KRASG12R expression at the mRNA and protein level (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to a strong suppression of dsRed::KRASG12R expression at the protein level.
source: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to a strong suppression of dsRed::KRASG12R expression at the mRNA and protein level (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to marked antiproliferative effects in MIA PaCa-2 cells.
source: ARTi-shRNAmir induction led to a strong suppression of dsRed::KRASG12R expression at the mRNA and protein level (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D) and marked antiproliferative effects (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ARTi-mediated suppression of KRASG12R led to full tumor regression in the absence of KRASG12C in xenograft experiments.
source: In xenograft experiments, ARTi-mediated suppression of KRASG12R led to full tumor regression in the absence of KRASG12C (Figure 2H)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Tumors harboring both KRASG12R and KRASG12C oncogenic alleles only displayed a delay in tumor progression upon ARTi-mediated suppression of KRASG12R.
source: while tumors harboring both oncogenic KRAS alleles only displayed a delay in tumor progression, suggesting that both oncogenes contribute to tumor growth in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data comparing tumors with different KRAS allele combinations.

claim: Both KRASG12R and KRASG12C oncogenes contribute to tumor growth in vivo.
source: while tumors harboring both oncogenic KRAS alleles only displayed a delay in tumor progression, suggesting that both oncogenes contribute to tumor growth in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tumors with both alleles showed delayed progression rather than full regression.

claim: Suppression of STAG1 in STAG2-deficient HCT 116 cells impaired their proliferation in vitro.
source: Suppression of STAG1 in STAG2-deficient HCT 116 cells impaired their proliferation in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Suppression of STAG1 in STAG2-deficient HCT 116 cells impaired the progression of xenografted tumors in vivo.
source: Suppression of STAG1 in STAG2-deficient HCT 116 cells impaired their proliferation in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) and the progression of xenografted tumors in vivo (Figure 2L)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir had no antiproliferative effects in HCT 116 cells in the presence of STAG2.
source: while dox-induced expression of the ARTi-shRNAmir had no antiproliferative effects in the presence of STAG2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing STAG2-wildtype and STAG2-deficient cells.

claim: ARTi is a versatile and precise LOF method for target validation in oncology and beyond.
source: Together, these studies establish ARTi as a versatile and precise LOF method for target validation in oncology and beyond.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental results demonstrating ARTi's effectiveness across multiple targets.

claim: ARTi provides full control over on- and off-target effects.
source: Instead of designing gene-specific LOF reagents that remain prone to off-target effects, ARTi involves a simple, highly standardized experimental procedure that provides full control over on- and off-target effects and can be applied to any coding and non-coding gene.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the design of ARTi, which uses pre-validated shRNAs and allows side-by-side comparison with wildtype cells.

claim: ARTi can be applied to any coding and non-coding gene.
source: Instead of designing gene-specific LOF reagents that remain prone to off-target effects, ARTi involves a simple, highly standardized experimental procedure that provides full control over on- and off-target effects and can be applied to any coding and non-coding gene.
evidence: The claim is based on the design principle of ARTi, which involves engineering target sites rather than targeting endogenous sequences.

claim: Placement of ARTi target sites in non-coding transcript regions leaves the endogenous target protein unaltered.
source: Placement of ARTi target sites in non-coding transcript regions leaves the endogenous target protein unaltered, which is a key advantage over chemical-genetic LOF methods relying on the introduction of degron tags (Lai and Crews, 2017; Cromm and Crews, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on the design principle of ARTi and is compared to degron-based methods via citations.

claim: Targeting endogenously engineered ARTi target sites through tetracycline-inducible ARTi-shRNAmir expression enables inducible, titratable, and likely reversible LOF perturbations.
source: Targeting endogenously engineered ARTi target sites through tetracycline (Tet)-inducible ARTi-shRNAmir expression enables inducible, titratable, and likely reversible (not tested in this study) LOF perturbations of candidate genes without altering their endogenous transcriptional regulation, which is not possible using conventional Tet-expression systems.
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the ARTi system using Tet-inducible expression, though reversibility was not experimentally tested.

claim: ARTi enables combinatorial LOF perturbations by engineering multiple target sites in the same cell.
source: In principle, by engineering multiple target sites in the same cell, ARTi enables combinatorial LOF perturbations, for example, for modeling synergistic target interactions, without multiplying the risk for off-target effects.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the principle of ARTi design but not experimentally demonstrated in this study.

claim: ARTi can be used to establish on-target benchmark phenotypes for guiding the development and optimization of inhibitory molecules.
source: Beyond providing a scalable method for early target validation, we foresee that ARTi can be used to establish on-target benchmark phenotypes for guiding the development and optimization of inhibitory molecules.
evidence: The claim is speculative, representing a potential future application of ARTi.

claim: Top-scoring siRNA predictions with DSIR score >105 harboring G or C in position 20 were analyzed for nucleotide biases.
source: To establish the criteria for ARTi design, siRNA predictions for the human and mouse genome were retrieved from DSIR (Vert et al., 2006) using default parameters. Top-scoring predictions (DSIR score >105) harboring G or C in position 20 were analyzed for nucleotide biases, which were used to define basic design criteria at the 5′-end the 3′-half.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach used to design ARTi shRNAs.

claim: Seed sequences with the lowest predicted off-target activity (top 1%) showed biases for C and/or G in guide positions 2–6.
source: Seed sequences with the lowest predicted off-target activity (top 1%) showed biases for C and/or G in guide positions 2–6, but 23% contained a T at the 5′ end of the seed sequence that is required in our design (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of siSPOTR predictions, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 73% of seed sequences with a 5′ T harbored CG in the following two positions.
source: Among these, we observed particularly strong biases for CG in the following two positions (Figure 1B), which were found in 73% of all seed sequences harboring a 5′ T.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of seed sequence composition, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 17% of all top-scoring seed sequences harbored TCG at their 5′ end.
source: Overall, 17% of all top-scoring seed sequences harbored TCG at their 5′ end, making it the second most common triplet (after CGC, which was found in 20%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of seed sequence composition.

claim: CGC was the most common triplet at the 5′ end of top-scoring seed sequences, found in 20%.
source: Overall, 17% of all top-scoring seed sequences harbored TCG at their 5′ end, making it the second most common triplet (after CGC, which was found in 20%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of seed sequence composition.

claim: The first four nucleotides of the ARTi guide were fixed to TTCG.
source: Based on these analyses, we fixed the first four nucleotides of the guide to TTCG.
evidence: The claim describes a design decision made by the authors based on their analyses.

claim: PC-9 cells are human EGFRdel19-dependent lung adenocarcinoma cells.
source: We introduced this construct into human EGFRdel19-dependent PC-9 lung adenocarcinoma cells and subsequently knocked out the endogenous EGFR gene.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing the cell line used.

claim: MIA PaCa-2 cells are KRASG12C-dependent pancreatic adenocarcinoma cells.
source: To establish a suitable KRASG12R-driven model, we engineered a dsRed::KRASG12R-ARTi transgene and the dox-inducible ARTi-shRNAmir into KRASG12C-dependent MIA PaCa-2 pancreatic adenocarcinoma cells and subsequently knocked out endogenous KRAS alleles (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing the cell line used.

claim: HCT 116 cells are colon carcinoma cells.
source: To evaluate STAG1 as synthetic-lethal dependency that is relevant in a wide range of STAG2-deficient cancers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Bailey et al., 2021; van der Lelij et al., 2020; Benedetti et al., 2014; van der Lelij et al., 2017), we engineered an isogenic pair of STAG2-wildtype and -deficient HCT 116 colon carcinoma cells
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing the cell line used.

claim: Osimertinib is a clinically approved EGFR inhibitor.
source: To evaluate whether ARTi can recapitulate drug activities in vivo, we xenotransplanted EGFRdel19::V5::dsRed::ARTi engineered PC-9 cells harboring the dox-inducible ARTi-shRNAmir and treated recipient mice upon tumor formation with either dox or the clinically approved EGFR inhibitor osimertinib.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is based on established knowledge about osimertinib.

claim: AMG-510 is a KRASG12C inhibitor.
source: As expected, switching the driving oncogene from KRASG12C to KRASG12R rendered MIA PaCa-2 cells resistant to the KRASG12C inhibitor AMG-510 (Fakih et al., 2020; Lanman et al., 2020; Fakih et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations to studies on AMG-510.

claim: There are no available in vivo compatible inhibitors for KRASG12R.
source: In a second study, we used ARTi to investigate KRASG12R, an oncogenic KRAS variant with no available in vivo compatible inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and represents the current state of drug development.
